review.facts: PubMed 25040456 abstract (Delmore, Irwin 2014): divides are zones between populations routing around unsuitable areas; geolocators on hybrid Swainson's thrushes in western Canada; more variable routes, some crossing arid and mountainous regions, some using one parental route in fall and the other in spring; selection against hybrids

band7.why: Two steps (parental routes avoid the interior, so hybrids' routes are riskier; fewer surviving hybrids help keep the groups apart). B keeps the true crossing and draws the wrong lesson, C keeps the more direct path and fails on timing. Band 6.

items.subtype: T2 intended readers: a printer's format choices reveal whom he expected to buy his books
items.passage: In the late fifteenth century, printed editions of classical authors frequently appeared in large formats, with the ancient text often surrounded by extensive scholarly commentary: volumes better suited to a desk or lectern than to travel. In 1501, however, the Venetian printer Aldus Manutius published the poetry of Virgil as a compact octavo volume, set in a new slanted typeface cut by the punchcutter Francesco Griffo—the first italic—and printed without any commentary whatsoever. Aldus promoted such books as portable, and although they were moderately priced for the time, they were by no means inexpensive. Considered together, Aldus’s decisions suggest that he anticipated purchasers who ______
options: had little money to spend on books and were willing to give up scholars’ notes in exchange for the lowest possible price.
were just beginning to study Latin and needed shortened versions of Virgil’s poems to prepare for lessons with a teacher.
could make sense of the ancient texts without scholars’ guidance and wanted books that they could easily carry with them.
found the new italic type easier to read than the type used in large volumes, which had become difficult to see clearly.
items.explanation: Aldus printed Virgil “without any commentary,” so his buyers would have to read the poems without scholars’ help, and he made the book small and “promoted such books as portable,” unlike volumes “suited to a desk or lectern.” Since the books were “by no means inexpensive,” the buyers were not simply looking for a bargain: they were readers able to manage the texts alone who wanted to carry them.

A.why_wrong: The books did lack scholars’ notes, but the text says they were “by no means inexpensive,” so the lowest possible price was not the attraction.

B.why_wrong: The book was small, not shortened: the text says Aldus published “the poetry of Virgil,” and beginners would be the readers most in need of the commentary he left out.

D.why_wrong: The text says only that the italic was new; it makes no claim about how easy it was to read or about any difficulty reading large volumes.

sources.what: Wikipedia, Aldus Manutius: libelli portatiles (portable small books); books published without commentary and in smaller sizes, usually octavos; the 1501 Virgil introduced italic print, designed for the pocket-sized classics; moderately priced but not cheap; he jettisoned commentary because he felt it prevented the dialogue between author and reader; a boon to scholars

items.notes: Area: humanities (book history). S9 hard, T2: three design facts (no commentary, small portable format, not cheap) must be combined; each distractor uses one of them wrongly (price, size as abridgment, the italic). The large-format, commentary-heavy norm before Aldus is general background, stated softly ("many", "often").
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

review.facts: Wikipedia Aldus Manutius: publishers often added commentary, making large books hard to transport; Aldine books without commentary and in smaller sizes, usually octavos; libelli portatiles; moderately priced but not cheap; the 1501 Virgil the first complete book in italic, type cut by Francesco Griffo

band7.why: Three design facts must be combined (no commentary, portable, not cheap). A keeps the missing notes and fails on price, B keeps the small size and fails on abridgment, D keeps the new italic. A dies to one phrase, so low end of band 6.

items.subtype: T3 consequence: praise with opposite effects in two groups, combined with who receives it most
items.passage: Adults frequently respond to children’s accomplishments with inflated praise (“That’s not just beautiful—that’s incredibly beautiful!”), often intending to bolster the children’s self-esteem. Psychologist Eddie Brummelman and colleagues found that adults are especially inclined to offer such praise to children with low self-esteem. In a subsequent experiment, children received either inflated or ordinary praise for a drawing and then chose between simpler and more difficult drawing tasks: inflated praise made children with high self-esteem more likely to attempt the difficult task but made children with low self-esteem less likely to do so. These findings suggest that adults who give inflated praise ______
options: tend to help children with low self-esteem more than children with high self-esteem, since the former receive more of that praise.
may most often give it to the very children whom it is least likely to encourage to take on challenges.
may discourage children with high self-esteem from seeking challenges, since such praise sets standards those children feel they must meet.
would encourage more children to seek challenges if they praised the effort children put into their work rather than its quality.
items.explanation: Adults are “especially inclined to offer such praise to children with low self-esteem,” yet inflated praise made those same children “less likely” to take on the harder task, while it encouraged children with high self-esteem. So the children who receive inflated praise most often are the ones it is least likely to push toward challenges.

A.why_wrong: Children with low self-esteem do receive more of the praise, but the experiment shows it made them less likely to take on challenges, so it did not help them more.

C.why_wrong: The text says inflated praise made children with high self-esteem more likely, not less likely, to take on the harder task; the discouraging effect was in the other group.

D.why_wrong: The experiment compared inflated with ordinary praise of a drawing; praise for effort was never tested.

sources.what: Brummelman, Thomaes, Orobio de Castro, Overbeek, Bushman 2014, Psychological Science 25:728 (PubMed abstract): adults especially inclined to give inflated praise to children with low self-esteem; inflated praise decreases challenge seeking in children with low self-esteem and has the opposite effect on children with high self-esteem

items.notes: Area: social science (developmental psychology). S7 hard: two groups with opposite outcomes (the conditional), joined to a second finding about which group gets the praise; the key needs both. Easier and harder drawing tasks simplified from the study's picture-copying choice. Distractors: REV, MIX (groups swapped), OUT (effort praise, attractive from background knowledge).
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

review.facts: PubMed 24434235 abstract (Brummelman et al. 2014): adults especially inclined to give inflated praise to children with low self-esteem; inflated praise decreases challenge seeking in children with low self-esteem and has the opposite effect in children with high self-esteem

band7.why: Two findings must be joined (who gets inflated praise, whom it discourages). A keeps the true first half (low self-esteem children get more of it) and fails on its effect, C swaps the groups, D is the familiar effort-praise idea. Band 6.

items.subtype: T1 revision: celebrated improvisations built from recurring figures relocate their originality
items.passage: Jazz improvisation is often characterized as the spontaneous invention of melody, and the solos of saxophonist Charlie Parker, celebrated since the 1940s for their inventiveness, have long been regarded as a model of that ideal. In a 1974 study of Parker’s recordings, however, musicologist Thomas Owens identified roughly a hundred short melodic figures that recur from solo to solo across many different tunes, and a 2018 computer analysis of 56 transcribed Parker solos by Klaus Frieler confirmed that Parker constructed his improvised lines almost entirely from such recurring patterns. These findings suggest that ______
options: the originality admired in Parker’s playing may have lain less in creating each phrase anew than in how he selected and combined familiar ones.
Parker likely composed and memorized most of his solos well before performing them, rather than improvising them as he played.
Parker probably relied on recurring melodic patterns far more heavily than other jazz saxophonists of the 1940s did when they improvised solos.
listeners who praised Parker’s inventiveness during the 1940s were probably unaware that many of the same short figures appeared in solo after solo.
items.explanation: Parker’s solos are “celebrated since the 1940s for their inventiveness,” yet he “constructed his improvised lines almost entirely from such recurring patterns.” If the phrases themselves recur, the inventiveness cannot lie mainly in new phrases; it more likely lies in how he chose and joined the figures he already had.

B.why_wrong: Reusing short figures “across many different tunes” is not the same as fixing whole solos in advance; the findings concern the building blocks, not prepared performances.

C.why_wrong: Both studies examined only Parker’s solos, so they say nothing about how other saxophonists of the time compared.

D.why_wrong: The text says nothing about what Parker’s listeners knew; it reports only what later analyses of his recordings found.

sources.what: Frieler 2018, Patternology: Melodic Pattern Usage in Charlie Parker's Solos (IRCAM talk abstract, Dig That Lick project): replicates and extends Thomas Owens's seminal work on Parker's use of patterns; algorithmic analysis of 56 Omnibook transcriptions supports Owens's finding that Parker makes extensive and nearly exclusive use of patterns. Owens 1974, Charlie Parker: Techniques of Improvisation (UCLA dissertation), about 100 principal motives

items.notes: Area: humanities (music). S11 hard: received view (invention in the moment, with Parker as its model) plus counterevidence (recurring figures); the key reconciles both facts rather than discarding one. Distractors: EXT (pre-composed solos), CMP (other players), OUT (listeners' awareness). The "about a hundred" figure is Owens's own count as quoted from his front matter; rounded.
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

review.facts: IRCAM talk abstract (Frieler 2018, Patternology): replicates Thomas Owens's work; algorithmic pattern extraction on 56 Omnibook transcriptions; Parker makes extensive and nearly exclusive use of patterns to construct his solos

band7.why: Received view and counterevidence reconciled rather than one discarded, key paraphrased. B overreaches from recurring figures to memorized solos, C invents a comparison with other players, D an unsupported claim about listeners. Band 6.

items.subtype: T1 revision: historical references to two sleeps undercut the single-stretch norm
items.passage: Sleeping in a single uninterrupted stretch each night is widely regarded as the natural human pattern. Historian Roger Ekirch, however, has assembled more than 500 references, in documents ranging from antiquity to the modern era, to a “first sleep” and a “second sleep” separated by roughly an hour of wakefulness around midnight, an interval that people devoted to prayer, to reflection on their dreams, or even to visits with neighbors. Ekirch attributes the disappearance of this pattern primarily to the spread of electric lighting. His findings suggest that ______
options: people who sleep in one stretch today probably sleep less deeply than people in earlier centuries who slept in two stretches did.
the hour of wakefulness between the two sleeps was mainly a result of people’s fears about crime and danger at night.
sleeping straight through the night may be a fairly recent habit rather than the only pattern that is natural to humans.
electric lighting has made it impossible for people today to sleep in two separate periods during the night.
items.explanation: The received view treats one “uninterrupted stretch” as natural, but Ekirch found “more than 500 references” to a “first sleep” and a “second sleep” across many centuries, and he ties the change to “the spread of electric lighting.” This suggests that sleeping in one stretch may be a recent habit, not the only natural pattern.

A.why_wrong: The text says nothing about how deeply people slept in either pattern.

B.why_wrong: The text describes what people did while awake, such as praying and visiting neighbors, but gives no cause for the waking period, and fear of crime is never mentioned.

D.why_wrong: Ekirch links electric lighting to “the disappearance of this pattern”; that does not mean sleeping in two periods has become impossible.

sources.what: Wikipedia, Biphasic and polyphasic sleep (Ekirch section): A. Roger Ekirch found more than 500 references to a segmented sleeping pattern (first sleep and second sleep) in documents from the ancient, medieval and modern world; waking interval used to pray, reflect, interpret dreams, visit neighbors; he attributes its disappearance to modern electric lighting

items.notes: Area: history (social history). S11 medium: received view plus counterevidence; one step to the revised view. Distractors: CMP, CAUSE, EXT (the hedge "most people" turned into impossibility).
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

review.facts: Wikipedia Polyphasic sleep (Ekirch passage, reached via the cited redirect): more than 500 references to segmented sleep in ancient, medieval and modern documents; waking used to pray, reflect, interpret dreams, visit neighbors; Ekirch ties its loss to modern electric lighting

items.subtype: T1 revision: emigration demand raised the number of nurses at home
items.passage: When health workers leave poorer countries for jobs in wealthier ones, their home countries are often thought to suffer a “brain drain,” and fears of such losses have led to calls to limit the international recruitment of nurses and doctors. In 2000, the United States greatly expanded the number of visas available to foreign nurses. Economists Paolo Abarcar and Caroline Theoharides found that nursing enrollment and graduation in the Philippines rose sharply in response: for each Filipino nurse who emigrated, approximately nine additional nurses became licensed in the Philippines. This finding suggests that ______
options: the visa expansion led many Filipino nurses who had planned to emigrate to stay in the Philippines instead.
the opportunity to work abroad may have added to, rather than reduced, the number of licensed nurses in the Philippines.
countries hoping to improve their health care should encourage as many of their nurses as possible to go to work abroad.
the nurses who became licensed in the Philippines after 2000 were more highly trained than those who emigrated.
items.explanation: The brain-drain view expects emigration to shrink a country’s supply of health workers. But “for each Filipino nurse who emigrated, approximately nine additional nurses became licensed in the Philippines.” Because more nurses were added than left, the chance to work abroad may have increased the number of nurses in the Philippines.

A.why_wrong: The visa expansion made emigration easier, and nurses did move abroad; the text describes more people entering nursing, not would-be emigrants staying home.

C.why_wrong: The study counted licensed nurses; it does not show that sending as many nurses abroad as possible would improve health care.

D.why_wrong: The text compares the numbers of nurses, not their training, so it gives no basis for judging which group was more highly trained.

sources.what: Abarcar and Theoharides, World Bank People Move blog, Brain gain: providing healthcare workers opportunities to migrate can increase education (study published in Review of Economics and Statistics 2024): in 2000 the US dramatically expanded visas for foreign nurses; nursing enrollment and graduation in the Philippines increased substantially; for each new nurse who moved abroad, nine additional nurses were licensed; new nurses passed the licensure exam at lower rates

items.notes: Area: social science (development economics). S11 medium: received view (brain drain) plus counterevidence (nine licensed per migrant). D is also contradicted by the study's lower pass rates (left out of the passage). Distractors: REV, REC, CMP.
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

review.facts: World Bank People Move blog (Abarcar, Theoharides 2021): US expanded nurse visas in 2000; Philippine nursing enrollment and graduation rose sharply; for each new nurse who moved abroad, nine additional nurses were licensed

items.subtype: T3 prediction: if a ban caused the raids, lifting it should reduce them
items.passage: In 1371 the founder of China’s Ming dynasty issued a maritime prohibition, or haijin, that made private commerce with foreign countries punishable by death; overseas trade was to pass only through official tribute missions. Trade abroad nevertheless remained profitable, and many coastal merchants and sailors whose livelihoods the prohibition had destroyed turned to smuggling and piracy, so that most of the pirates who raided China’s coastline were themselves Chinese. If the raids were largely a consequence of the prohibition, then the court’s decision in 1567 to begin issuing permits for most private overseas trade would most likely have ______
options: increased piracy along the coast, since the permits drew more foreign ships into Chinese waters.
ended the tribute system, since official missions would no longer be needed to carry on overseas trade.
led the court to make smuggling a capital crime, since smugglers could no longer claim that trade was forbidden.
reduced piracy along the coast, since many who had turned to raiding could again earn a living through legal trade.
items.explanation: The raiders were mostly people “whose livelihoods the prohibition had destroyed.” If the raids were largely a consequence of the prohibition, permits for private trade would give those people a lawful way to earn a living again, so piracy would most likely decline.

A.why_wrong: The text traces the raids to the ban on trade, not to foreign ships, so reopening trade would be expected to reduce piracy, not increase it.

B.why_wrong: The text says nothing about what happened to the tribute missions; permitting private trade need not have ended official missions.

C.why_wrong: Private foreign trade was already “punishable by death” under the 1371 ban, so the court did not first make it a capital crime in 1567.

items.notes: Area: history (Ming China). S2 medium with a conditional lead-in ("If the raids were largely a product of the ban"), as in the official 3.33 frame. The key matches the recorded outcome. "Most private overseas trade" covers the exception for Japan.
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

items.subtype: T5 status: a coin that could have arrived by Indigenous trade does not prove a Norse visit
items.passage: In 1957 an amateur archaeologist reported discovering a Norwegian silver coin at the Goddard site in Maine, an extensive Native American settlement occupied from approximately 1180 to 1235. The coin was minted between 1065 and 1080, during the reign of King Olaf Kyrre, and some commentators have interpreted it as evidence that Norse voyagers reached the coast of Maine. However, excavations at the site also recovered a stone tool produced by the Dorset culture, whose people inhabited regions far to the north, suggesting that certain objects arrived at the settlement from distant places through trade networks. Therefore, ______
options: the coin’s presence at the site is not conclusive evidence that Norse voyagers ever traveled as far south as Maine.
the coin was most likely made at the site by local people who copied the designs of Norwegian coins.
the Dorset people probably traded directly with Norwegian merchants who sailed to North America during the reign of King Olaf Kyrre.
the coin must have been left at the site by Norse voyagers sometime between 1065 and 1080.
items.explanation: Some have “interpreted it as evidence that Norse voyagers reached the coast of Maine,” but the Dorset tool suggests that “certain objects arrived at the settlement from distant places through trade networks.” The coin could have arrived the same way, so it does not settle whether the Norse came to Maine.

B.why_wrong: The text identifies the coin as “Norwegian” and gives its minting dates; nothing suggests it was a local copy.

C.why_wrong: The text shows only that objects traveled through trade; it gives no evidence of direct contact between Dorset people and Norwegian merchants.

D.why_wrong: The Dorset tool raises another way the coin could have arrived, and the settlement was occupied only from about 1180, more than a century after the coin was minted.

items.notes: Area: history (archaeology). S5 medium: evidence for a Norse visit plus an equally good rival route (Indigenous trade). The passage says "reported finding" because some numismatists doubt the find; the item does not depend on that question.
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

items.subtype: T4 function: oxygen falling in a rebreathed bubble shows the bubble is breathed
items.passage: Several semiaquatic species of anoles, lizards that inhabit streamside forests in Central and South America, dive to escape predators and can remain submerged for as long as 18 minutes. While underwater, these lizards repeatedly exhale a bubble of air that adheres to their snouts and subsequently inhale it again. Biologist Christopher Boccia and colleagues measured the oxygen concentration in these bubbles and found that it decreased the longer a lizard remained submerged, whereas the oxygen in bubbles attached to lifeless mechanical models did not decrease. These measurements indicate that the bubble ______
options: mainly protects the lizards’ eyes and nostrils from the debris that fast-moving streams carry along.
is a store of air that the lizards actually breathe, which may help them stay hidden underwater for longer.
is a sign that a lizard is running out of air and will need to return to the surface within seconds.
takes in oxygen from the surrounding water faster than the lizards use it, so its oxygen supply keeps rising.
items.explanation: The oxygen in the bubbles “decreased the longer a lizard remained submerged,” but not in bubbles on “lifeless mechanical models,” so the living lizards were using the bubble’s oxygen. Since the lizards “dive to escape predators,” breathing this air may let them stay hidden longer.

A.why_wrong: The study measured the bubble’s oxygen, which fell only with living lizards; nothing in the text concerns debris or protecting the eyes.

C.why_wrong: The lizards breathe the bubble “repeatedly” and can stay under “for as long as 18 minutes,” so the bubble is not a sign of an imminent return to the surface.

D.why_wrong: The text says the oxygen in the bubbles “decreased,” not that it kept rising.
